title: Wigner negativity and stellar rank for SU(1,1) states
authors: A. B. Klimov, A. Muñoz, F. Leuchs, J. -P. Gazeau, L. L. Sanchez-Soto
abstract: Quasiprobability distributions for systems endowed with SU(1,1) dynamical symmetry have received surprisingly little attention, despite the central role of this symmetry in two-photon physics, squeezed states, and nonlinear interferometry. Here, we fill this gap by constructing a full covariant family of $s$-ordered quasiprobability distributions defined on the two-sheeted hyperboloid, or equivalently, on the Poincaré unit disk via stereographic projection. A key result is that the Wigner function is strictly positive for all Perelomov SU(1,1) coherent states, in sharp contrast to the SU(2) case. This positivity endows Wigner negativity with an unambiguous operational meaning: any negative volume is a direct signature of genuinely quantum behavior. We further examine the stellar rank of SU(1,1) states, defined through the zeros of the Husimi $Q$-function, and show how it compares with Wigner negativity as a geometry-adapted witness of nonclassicality in this setting. We further introduce a hierarchy of generalized multipoles through a harmonic expansion of the density operator on the hyperboloid, providing a complementary framework for probing quantumness. This offers a comprehensive toolkit for characterizing and quantifying quantum resources in SU(1,1) systems.
summary: This paper develops advanced phase-space tools to measure quantumness in systems possessing SU(1,1) symmetry. It establishes that Wigner negativity is a reliable indicator of nonclassicality for these systems, contrasting with other symmetries. By combining this with generalized multipole expansions, the authors offer a comprehensive mathematical toolkit for characterizing quantum states.
main_problem: The goal is to systematically characterize and quantify quantum resources (quantumness) for systems governed by SU(1,1) dynamical symmetry using phase-space methods.
main_result: For SU(1,1) systems, Wigner negativity serves as an unambiguous sufficient witness of nonclassicality because the Wigner function remains strictly positive for all coherent states. The analysis provides a comprehensive toolkit combining Wigner negativity and generalized multipoles.
method: The authors construct covariant quasiprobability distributions on the two-sheeted hyperboloid and analyze quantumness using spectral methods, harmonic expansions, and comparisons between different state representations (e.g., cat states vs. coherent states).
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum systems exhibiting SU(1,1) dynamical symmetry. The phase space is modeled by the two-sheeted hyperboloid or Poincaré unit disk, utilizing Perelomov SU(1,1) coherent states.
key_observables: Wigner negativity (negative volume), Stellar Rank (zeros of the Husimi Q-function), and generalized multipole strengths ($q_{\varrho}(k, \lambda)$).
important_parameters: The analysis involves parameters related to the excitation number ($n$), hyperbolic coordinates ($\zeta$), and spectral indices ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of harmonic function theory on the hyperboloid and relies on comparing state properties against those of coherent states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate density plots of harmonic functions, Wigner functions for various states (coherent, basis, cat), and plots showing multipole norms ($q$) versus spectral index ($\lambda$).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the covariant quasiprobability framework on the hyperboloid. It then analyzes key diagnostics like Wigner negativity and stellar rank, introduces generalized multipoles via harmonic expansion, and finally applies these tools to specific quantum states (e.g., cat states) to quantify nonclassicality.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework for quantifying quantum resources in systems with hyperbolic symmetries, offering an alternative diagnostic tool beyond standard quadrature measurements relevant to quantum optics and field theory.
